question: to the Commission Nicola Zingaretti (S&D), Sandro Ruotolo (S&D), Irene Tinagli (S&D), Giorgio Gori (S&D), Brando Benifei (S&D), Georgia Tramacere (S&D), Alessandro Zan (S&D) Subject:

In a potential infringement of Directive 1999/70/EC, the Italian National Institute of Astrophysics (INAF) employs some 37 % of its staff on fixed-term contracts. Around 300 workers meet the requirements to be made permanent within the meaning of Article 20 of Legislative Decree No 75/2017 (‘Madia Law’), which expires on 31 December 2026. They are professionals with an average age of 40 who were precariously employed for 8 to 10 years after they received their doctorates. Law No 199/2025 and Ministerial Decree No 195 of 5 March 2026 (Ministry of Universities and Research (MUR) Distribution Decree) allocate only EUR 1.7 million to the recruitment of INAF staff, compared with the EUR 6.5 million proposed by the MUR in June 2025, covering a small proportion of eligible staff. The same provision excludes a significant proportion of longer-term temporary workers who are paid by means of research cheques or non-National Recovery and Resilience Plan funds. Without action, more than 100 researchers – whose training was paid for through NRRP and Horizon Europe funds, among others (Regulation (EU) 2021/695) – will be forced to leave the system by the end of the year. In the light of the above: 1.
Does the Commission consider the levels of precarious employment at INAF compatible with Directive 1999/70/EC?
What steps will it take to prevent EU funds from perpetuating structural precariousness?
Will it make future research disbursements conditional on compliance with fair employment standards, including under the European Pillar of Social Rights?

(3 July 2026) Council Directive 1999/70/EC (1) does not lay down limits on the share of fixed-term contracts in specific sectors but requires Member States to adopt measures to prevent misuse of successive fixed-term employment contracts, in taking account of the needs of specific sectors (2). The Commission is closely monitoring Member States’ compliance, having regard to the case law of the Court of Justice (3). The Commission is committed to ensuring that disbursements of EU research funds under the Recovery and Resilience Fund are conditional on compliance with fair employment standards, in line with the European Pillar of Social Rights. Italy’s national Recovery and Resilience Plan includes reforms aimed at supporting research institutions, as a prerequisite for receiving instalments (4). Likewise, Horizon Europe (5) (HE) promotes attractive and sustainable careers for researchers, including through requirements (6) in line with the European framework for research careers and the principles of the European Charter for Researchers (7).

http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/1999/70/oj. The directive assigns to the Member States the general objective of preventing such abuse, while leaving them discretion as to how to achieve it. The Court of Justice has clarified that the framework Agreement on fixed-term work does not lay down a general obligation on the Member States to provide for the conversion of fixed-term employment contracts into contracts of indefinite duration, confer, e.g., judgment of 8 March 2012, Martial Huet v Université de Bretagne occidentale, C-251/11, EU:2012:133, paragraph 38, https://infocuria.curia.europa.eu/tabs/document? source=document&text=&docid=120125&pageIndex=0&doclang=EN&mode=lst&dir=&occ=first&part=1&cid=3435083. Concerning researchers’ careers in Italy, the Court has for instance ruled that Clause 5 of the framework Agreement on fixed-term work must be interpreted as not precluding national legislation which sets the total duration of the employment contracts that may be concluded by a single researcher, including with different universities and institutes, at 12 years, confer judgment of 15 December 2022, AQ and Others v Presidenza del Consiglio dei ministri and Others, C40/20, EU:C:2022:985, https://juris.curia.europa.eu/juris/document/document.jsf? text=&docid=268607&pageIndex=0&doclang=en&mode=lst&dir=&occ=first&part=1&cid=3381762. Specifically, one key reform focuses on enhancing the stability and transparency of research funding, by establishing a binding legal framework for a threeyear rolling plan that allocates predictable, multi-annual funding for research activities. If Italy fails to implement such reforms adequately, the Commission may withhold payments until corrective measures are taken. https://research-and-innovation.ec.europa.eu/funding/funding-opportunities/funding-programmes-and-open-calls/horizon-europe_en. According to Article 18 of Annex 5 to the Horizon Europe General Model Grant Agreement, beneficiaries must take all measures to implement the principles of the European Charter for Researchers and must ensure that researchers and all participants involved in the action are aware of them. https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/C/2023/1640/oj/eng

Moreover, the same framework recommends that Member States counter the phenomenon of precarity and support job security and stability (8). A Mutual Learning Exercise supported by HE allowed Member States to exchange good practices on research careers, including to fight precarity (9). Generally, in the context of funds managed under the shared management principle, such as the European Social Fund plus, the Commission verifies (10) that the managing authority takes the necessary steps to ensure that projects are in line with the objectives of the programme and with the cohesion policy.
